AIDA model for social media ads: how to map each stage to formats and metrics

Illustration: AIDA model for social media ads: how to map each stage to formats and metrics

The AIDA model (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action) works on social media ads when you treat each stage as a job with its own format and its own metric. Attention is won in the first second of the feed, Interest in the next few seconds, Desire through proof and an offer, and Action through one clear next step. When results are weak, the metric for each stage tells you which job is failing.
On social media, all four AIDA stages often happen inside one ad, so plan the ad second by second.
Give each stage one metric, so you can see where people drop off.
Most weak ads fail at Attention or Desire, not at Action.
Use different formats for cold and warm audiences instead of one ad for everyone.
Test one stage at a time, or you will not know what changed the result.
Why does AIDA still matter for social ads?

AIDA gives a team a shared checklist for a short, crowded format. People scroll fast, and an ad that skips a stage usually loses them. Our <g1>AIDA model examples</g1> show the model across channels; this article applies it to paid social, where the stages are measured in seconds.
It is a simple model, not a law of buyer behaviour. Our comparison of <g1>AIDA with other funnels</g1> explains where it fits and where a fuller funnel is better.
How do you map each AIDA stage on a social ad?
Job in the ad
Formats that fit
Metric to watch
Stop the scroll in the first second
Short vertical video, a bold first frame, a face, motion
Share of impressions that become {1}-second video views
Make the viewer stay and understand
A clear problem in the first lines, captions, a quick demo
Average watch time, share of views that reach the middle
Make the offer feel worth it
Proof: reviews, results, before and after, creators
Link click-through rate, saves and shares
Make the next step easy
One call to action, a matching landing page, lead forms
Conversion rate after the click, cost per result
What does each stage need in practice?

<g1>Attention.</g1> Show the most interesting thing first. Put the product, the person or the result in the opening frame. Many people watch with the sound off, so add captions and make the first line readable at a glance.
<g1>Interest.</g1> Name the problem the viewer has, in their words. A short demo or a surprising fact keeps them watching. Keep one idea per ad.
<g1>Desire.</g1> Prove the claim. Reviews, numbers, creators who use the product, and a specific offer all build desire. Proof is where many ads are thin, because it takes real material to make.
<g1>Action.</g1> Ask for one thing. Repeat the call to action in the video, the caption and the button, and make sure the landing page continues the same message.
How do you find which stage is failing?

Read the metrics in order. If few people watch past the first seconds, fix Attention before anything else. If they watch but do not click, the problem is usually Interest or Desire: the message is unclear or the offer is weak. If they click but do not convert, look at Action and the landing page.

Change one stage per test. If you swap the hook, the proof and the offer at once, you cannot tell which change worked. For copy you can test, our <g1>AIDA copywriting templates</g1> include social versions.
Should cold and warm audiences see the same ad?

No. People who have never heard of you need more Attention and Interest. People who visited your site or engaged with your content already know you, so their ads can start at Desire, with proof and an offer. A simple setup is one awareness ad for cold audiences and one offer ad for warm audiences, each measured on its own stage metric.
How can competitor ads help you plan each stage?

Competitor ads show which hooks, proof and offers are already common in your category. If every rival opens with a discount, a hook built on a problem or a story will stand out. <g1>SOMIN Strategy</g1> tags competitor ads by message and format, so you can see which stages your category over-uses and where there is room for a different angle.
What is the AIDA model in social media marketing?
It is a four-stage checklist for an ad or post: win attention, build interest, create desire and prompt action. On social media the four stages often happen inside one short video.
Which AIDA stage matters most for social ads?
Attention, because nothing else happens if people scroll past. After that, Desire is the most common weak point, because many ads make a claim without proof.
Can one ad cover all four AIDA stages?
Yes, especially in short video. For cold audiences it is often better to split the job: one ad to earn attention and interest, and a second, retargeted ad for desire and action.
How long should each stage be in a video ad?
There is no fixed rule. A common pattern is a hook in the first second or two, the problem and idea next, proof in the middle and the call to action at the end. Test the timing on your own audience.

Generative engine optimisation (GEO): a brand checklist
Generative engine optimisation (GEO): a…
Illustration: Generative engine optimisation (GEO): a practical checklist for brand content

Generative engine optimisation (GEO) is the work of making your brand appear, and appear correctly, in answers from AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity. It builds on SEO: clear pages, consistent facts and trusted mentions. The difference is that AI systems summarise and cite, so you need content that answers questions directly and facts that agree everywhere.
Answer real questions in the first lines of a page, in plain language.
Keep company facts identical across your site, profiles and directories.
Use clear structure: headings as questions, short paragraphs, tables, FAQs and structured data.
Earn mentions on sites that AI systems cite, not just links.
Monitor what AI assistants say about you, and correct the sources behind wrong answers.
How is GEO different from SEO?

SEO aims for a ranking on a results page. GEO aims for inclusion in an answer. AI assistants with web search find pages, pull out passages and write a summary, often with citations. Pages that state a clear answer, with facts that are easy to extract and confirmed elsewhere, are easier to use. Our essay on <g1>the end of SEO and the agentic web</g1> explains the wider shift.
What is on the GEO checklist?
Start each page with a one-paragraph answer to the main question.
Write headings as the questions people ask, in their words and languages.
Give specific facts: numbers, dates, names, prices, with a source.
Add a short FAQ with complete, standalone answers.
Facts and entities
Use the same company name, description, founders, locations and product names everywhere.
Keep an "about" page and a press page with the canonical facts.
Update profiles on LinkedIn, review sites and directories when facts change.
Structure and access
Add structured data (schema.org) for your organisation, products, articles and FAQs.
Make sure pages render as text without scripts, load fast and are not blocked for the crawlers you want.
Consider an llms.txt file that points AI systems to your key pages.
Mentions
Get covered by trusted publications, research, reviews and industry lists in your category.
Publish original data that others will quote.
How do you measure AI visibility?

Write a fixed list of prompts that real buyers would ask, such as "best social listening tool for agencies in Southeast Asia". Run them in several assistants every month and record whether your brand appears, how it is described, which competitors appear and which sources are cited. Compare the cited sources with your own pages to find what is missing.
What do you do when an AI answer is wrong?

Find where the wrong fact comes from: an old page, a directory or an article. Fix your own pages first, then ask the other sites to update. Make the correct fact easy to find on your site, in text and in structured data. Expect changes to take weeks, because AI systems refresh their sources at different speeds.
Where does competitor research fit?

AI answers often compare brands. Knowing how competitors describe themselves, and which claims they repeat, shows where your positioning is unclear or crowded. <g1>SOMIN Strategy</g1> maps competitor messages across channels, which helps you choose claims that are both true and distinct.
What is GEO in marketing?
Generative engine optimisation: making content and facts easy for AI assistants to find, trust and cite, so your brand appears correctly in their answers.
No. AI assistants with web search still rely on pages that search engines can crawl. GEO adds answer-first writing, consistent facts and monitoring of AI answers.
How long does GEO take to work?
Weeks to months. Your pages need to be crawled, and AI systems refresh what they use at different speeds.
Can AI assistants make mistakes about my brand?
Yes. They can repeat outdated or wrong facts. Check regularly and fix the sources behind wrong answers.

Illustration: Open-source social listening tools: what they can do, and where they stop

Open-source social listening tools are free building blocks: code to collect public posts, libraries to analyse language, and dashboards to show the results. They suit teams with developers, a narrow question and a few sources. They stop at data access: the big platforms limit what can be collected, so coverage, history and upkeep become the real costs.
Open-source listening is a set of parts you assemble, not a ready product.
Data access, not software, is the hard part: platforms restrict and price their APIs.
Free software still costs developer time, hosting and maintenance.
Use open source for focused research; use a platform when you need many sources, markets and languages every week.
What does an open-source listening stack look like?
Typical open-source options
Collection
Gets posts and comments from sources
Official API clients, RSS readers, web scrapers where allowed
Storage
Keeps the data and its history
Open-source databases and search engines
Language detection, sentiment, topics, entities
Python NLP libraries and open language models
Shows trends and alerts
Open-source BI and charting tools
Where do open-source tools stop?

<g1>Access to data.</g1> The main platforms decide who can collect what. X ended free access to its API in {1} and moved to paid tiers, Reddit started charging for heavy API use the same year, and Meta shut down CrowdTangle in August {2}, pointing researchers to its Meta Content Library instead. Scraping can break platform terms. Open-source code does not solve these limits.
<g1>History.</g1> Most tools only see what you collect from the day you start. Paid platforms often hold archives.

<g1>Languages and images.</g1> Sentiment models trained mostly on English often miss slang, mixed languages and meaning carried by images or video. Our article on <g2>multilingual and visual AI social listening</g2> explains why.
<g1>Upkeep.</g1> APIs and page layouts change, and collectors break. Someone has to fix them.
What does "free" really cost?

Count developer time to build and maintain collectors, hosting and storage, paid API tiers, and the analyst time to check results. For a one-off study, this is often cheaper than a licence. For weekly reporting across several markets, the hidden costs add up. Our look at <g1>social listening pricing</g1> compares the cost models.
When is open source the right choice?
A research project with a clear question and a fixed time frame.
Sources with open access, such as news sites, forums, blogs or your own channels.
A team with developers who can maintain the stack.
Strict data rules that require everything to run on your own servers.
When does a platform pay off?

When you need many sources and markets, history, images and video, and results every week without maintaining code. Platforms also handle data agreements with the networks. Our list of the <g1>best social listening tools for agencies in {1}</g1> compares options. <g2>SOMIN Strategy</g2> combines listening with competitor ad tracking and audience insight, so the data turns into briefs, not just charts.
Are there free social listening tools?
Yes, as open-source software and free tiers. Open-source tools are free to use but need developers, hosting and data access.
Can open-source tools collect data from Instagram, TikTok or X?
Only within what each platform allows. Official APIs are limited or paid, and scraping can break platform terms.
Is open-source sentiment analysis accurate?
It can be good in English and on clean text. Accuracy drops with slang, mixed languages, sarcasm and images, so check samples by hand.
What replaced CrowdTangle?
Meta shut CrowdTangle down in August {1} and offers the Meta Content Library to approved researchers.

How to track social media algorithm changes
How to track social media algorithm changes…
Illustration: How to track social media algorithm changes without chasing rumours

To track social media algorithm changes, follow each platform's official explanations, keep a simple log of your own results, and test a suspected change before you react. Most "algorithm update" posts are guesses. A drop in reach can come from your content, your posting pattern, the season or competitors, so check those before you blame the platform.
Use official sources first: platform help pages, transparency pages and statements by platform leads.
Keep a weekly log of reach and engagement by format, so you can spot real shifts.
Compare with a benchmark, such as competitors in the same category, before you blame the algorithm.
Test a change on a small share of posts for a few weeks before you change the whole plan.
Where do platforms explain their ranking?

Each large platform publishes some explanation of how it ranks content. Meta has published system cards that describe how AI systems rank content on Facebook and Instagram, in its Transparency Center. TikTok explains how videos are recommended in its newsroom and help pages. YouTube describes its recommendations on its "How YouTube works" site, and LinkedIn's engineering team writes about its feed. Heads of platforms, such as Instagram's head Adam Mosseri, also share changes in their own posts and videos. These sources rarely give formulas, but they tell you which signals matter.
How do you tell a real change from noise?
<g1>Log the basics weekly:</g1> posts, reach, engagement and saves or shares, split by format (short video, image, carousel, text).
<g1>Look for a pattern across several weeks,</g1> not one bad post. A real shift shows up across many posts.
<g1>Check other causes:</g1> fewer posts, a new format, a holiday, a viral post the week before, or paid support ending.
<g1>Compare with peers.</g1> If competitors' reach fell at the same time, the cause is likely the platform or the season. If only yours fell, look at your content.
Our summary of <g1>social media algorithm changes in {1}</g1> lists the signals platforms have said they reward.
How should you test a suspected change?

Turn the rumour into a question you can test. For example: "Do carousels now reach more people than single images for us?" Post both formats on similar topics for three to four weeks, at similar times, and compare the median result, not the best post. If the difference is small, do not rebuild your plan around it.
What should you change, and what should you keep?

Platforms change details often, but some things hold: content that people watch to the end, save, share or reply to tends to travel further. Keep the parts of your plan that produce those reactions. Change the format mix only when your own data, not a rumour, shows a shift.
Why do competitor benchmarks matter?

Your own account is a small sample. Looking at what competitors post and how their content performs shows whether a format is rising across the category. <g1>SOMIN Strategy</g1> tracks competitor posts and ads by format and engagement, so you can compare your trend with the category's.
Constantly, in small ways. Platforms test and adjust ranking all the time and announce only some changes, which is why your own log matters.
My reach dropped this week. Is it the algorithm?
Not necessarily. Check your posting frequency, formats, timing, the season and competitors' reach first. One week is too short to call a trend.
Where can I find official information?
Platform help centres, transparency pages, engineering blogs and posts by platform leads. Treat third-party claims as hypotheses to test.
Should I change my strategy after every update?
No. Change your format mix when your own data shows a shift over several weeks.

AI community manager: what to automate and keep human
AI community manager: what to automate in…
Illustration: AI community manager: what to automate in comments and DMs, and what to keep human

An AI community manager is an agent that reads comments and direct messages, sorts them, drafts replies and sends the right ones to people. Automate the repetitive, low-risk work: tagging, routing, answers to common questions and first replies. Keep complaints, crises, legal or medical questions, influencer and press contacts, and anything emotional with a person.
Start with sorting and drafting, not with auto-posting.
Write the rules first: topics the agent may answer, topics it must pass on, and the tone it uses.
Give the agent approved answers to draw from, so it does not invent facts.
Measure response time and escalation quality, not just volume.
What can an AI community manager do?

It can do four jobs well. It sorts incoming comments and messages by topic, sentiment and urgency. It drafts replies from your approved answers. It routes messages to the right team, such as sales, support or PR. And it reports on what people are asking about, which is useful for content and product teams. Our overview of <g1>what AI social media manager agents can run</g1> covers the wider role.
Which replies should you automate?
Thank-you replies to positive comments
Complaints and refund requests
Opening hours, prices, links, stock questions
Anything about health, safety, legal or money advice
Hiding obvious spam and scams, following your policy
Crises, outages and viral negative threads
Tagging and routing DMs to the right team
Press, influencer and partnership messages
First reply to a support question with a next step
Upset or vulnerable people
A good middle ground is draft-and-approve: the agent writes the reply, a person clicks send. Move a topic to full automation only when its drafts have needed no edits for several weeks.
How do you set the rules before switching it on?
<g1>List the topics.</g1> Export a month of comments and DMs and group them. Most brands find a handful of topics make up most of the volume.
<g1>Write approved answers.</g1> One short answer per common question, with links. The agent should only state facts that are in these answers.
<g1>Define escalation.</g1> Name the words, topics and sentiment that send a message to a person, and who that person is.
<g1>Set the tone.</g1> Give examples of good replies in your brand voice, in each language you support.
<g1>Decide the hours.</g1> If people only review drafts in office hours, say so in the first auto-reply.
What should you measure?

Track time to first reply, the share of messages resolved without a person, the share of drafts edited before sending, and escalations that came too late. Read a sample of automated replies every week. A rising edit rate means the answers or rules need updating.
What are the risks?

The main risks are wrong facts, a tone that feels robotic, and replying to the wrong thing, such as a joke or sarcasm. Platforms also have their own rules for automated messaging, so check each platform's policies. Tell people when they are talking to an automated assistant if your market or platform expects it.

The <g1>SOMIN Social Media Manager</g1> plans and drafts content from competitor and audience data, and the questions people ask in your comments are one of the best inputs for that plan. See <g2>how the SOMIN social media manager agent works</g2>.

Will an AI community manager replace people?
It takes over repetitive replies and sorting. People still handle complaints, crises, partnerships and judgement calls, and they own the rules the agent follows.
Should replies be posted automatically?
Start with draft-and-approve. Automate a topic fully only after its drafts have been accurate for several weeks.
Can it reply in several languages?
Yes, but give it approved answers and tone examples in each language, and have a native speaker review samples.
